Good morning, Shahriaar. Today is Sunday, November 15. This is your morning brief.

Weather today is 7 degrees Celsius, overcast. The high will be 15 and the low 6 degrees Celsius. Chance of precipitation is 0 percent.

You have 2 appointments in the next 24 hours: 11:00 AM, Interview with Mr. Hossein Pour (LinkedIn); 3:00 PM, ghaemshahr-gorgan.

Now, the top 5 stories in AI today.

First, from TechCrunch: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang steps down. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has stepped down, according to the supplied coverage. The departure follows a period in which Nvidia's security chief quietly left in August, and reports connected Huang's relationships, including one with an executive at a company suspected of funneling chips to China, to security concerns. Why it matters: Major AI company leadership change with potential implications for AI infrastructure and geopolitical security.

Second, from WIRED: Beware the New AI-Fueled Ransomware Boom. WIRED reports that fully automated ransomware has not arrived yet, but seemingly unsophisticated attackers are using AI tools to wreak havoc. The development matters because AI may lower barriers for cyber attackers and increase real-world security risk. The supplied material does not detail specific attacks or defenses, but the trend is significant for enterprise security planning. Why it matters: Practical AI security threat that could affect enterprises.

Third, from WIRED: No Pilots, Few Air Traffic Controllers: What Could Go Wrong? WIRED reports that AI has come for the skies, even though aviation is normally slow to embrace new technology. The piece raises questions about AI use in aviation with no pilots and few air traffic controllers. It matters for practical safety and enterprise implications, though the supplied material does not provide full details about implementation or risks. Why it matters: AI applied to high-stakes physical infrastructure.

Fourth, from TechCrunch: The AI graveyard: a running list of AI projects and startups that did not make it. The article reviews AI projects and startups that shut down or missed expectations, including Apple's repeatedly delayed Siri AI and OpenAI's messy super app launch. It matters as a market reality check for AI investments and product expectations. The supplied material does not provide a full ranking or evaluation criteria. Why it matters: Highlights failed or underdelivered AI products.

Fifth, from The Verge: The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can’t trust AI CEOs. The Verge AI podcast features Helen Toner, OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman, discussing AI safety and policy. She says we still cannot trust AI CEOs. The development matters for AI governance and leadership accountability. The supplied material is limited to the interview description and does not include her full argument. Why it matters: Raises AI safety and governance questions.

That is your brief. Have a great day.
